clinicalPearls: Diverticulosis is the most common cause of hematochezia (brisk lower-GI bleed) in patients >60 years; bleeding is abrupt in onset, usually painless, sometimes massive, and often from the right colon. Chronic or occult bleeding is NOT characteristic (Harrison 22e p.2496, 2579).

Only ~20% of patients with diverticulosis will ever have GI bleeding; most bleeds are self-limited and stop spontaneously with bowel rest (colonic diverticula stop bleeding spontaneously in >=90% of patients). Lifetime risk of rebleeding is ~25% (Harrison 22e p.2496, 2579).
Acute uncomplicated diverticulitis characteristically presents with fever, anorexia, left lower quadrant abdominal pain, and obstipation (Harrison 22e p.2579).

Diagnosis of diverticulitis is best made on a contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT showing sigmoid diverticula, thickened colonic wall >4 mm, and pericolic fat inflammation WITHOUT extravasation of contrast or fluid (Harrison 22e p.2579).
Diverticula commonly affect the left and sigmoid colon and the rectum is always spared; however in Asian populations 70% of diverticula are in the right colon and cecum (Harrison 22e p.2579).

The pseudodiverticulum (protrusion of mucosa and submucosa only, through the muscularis propria) is the most common type seen in the colon; a true diverticulum is herniation of the entire bowel wall (Harrison 22e p.2578).

Perforated diverticular disease is staged using the Hinchey classification (I: confined paracolic abscess; II: distant/pelvic abscess after spontaneous closure; III: noncommunicating perforation with purulent peritonitis; IV: free perforation with fecal peritonitis); modified to add stage Ia for phlegmon/early abscess (Harrison 22e p.2580).

Pneumaturia or passage of stool/air through the vagina or skin signals a fistula (colovesical, colovaginal, or colocutaneous); colovaginal fistulas are more common in women who have undergone hysterectomy (Harrison 22e p.2579).

Colonoscopy should be considered ~6 weeks AFTER resolution of a first episode, because colon cancer prevalence is low overall (<2%) but higher after complicated diverticulitis (6-8%) (Harrison 22e p.2580).

Routine antibiotics do NOT shorten time to symptom resolution or reduce complications/recurrence in immunocompetent patients with uncomplicated diverticular disease (AVOD and DIABOLO trials, plus meta-analysis) (Harrison 22e p.2580).
Diverticulosis affects about half the population aged >60 years and the majority remain asymptomatic; only ~5% develop acute diverticular disease (Harrison 22e p.2578).
harrison.pathophysiology: Diverticula form where the nutrient artery (vasa recta) penetrates the muscularis propria, creating a point of weakness in the colonic wall; most arise in the sigmoid colon, likely reflecting its high-pressure zone where higher-amplitude contractions and firm/constipated stool act on a weak segment. Pathogenesis is now viewed as multifactorial rather than simply low-fiber diet: gut dysbiosis, chronic low-grade inflammation driving neuronal degeneration with resulting dysmotility and high intraluminal pressure, and abnormal collagen cross-linking causing loss of compliance all contribute. Genome-wide association studies (Iceland, Denmark, UK biobanks) link LAMB4 (extracellular-matrix laminin family) and TNFSF15 (TNF family, inflammation) variants to early-onset severe disease. Complications occur when the vasa recta is compressed or eroded (bleeding) or a diverticulum perforates (Harrison 22e p.2578-2579).
additionalDifferentials: Colorectal cancer (parallel epidemiology and overlapping presentation; must exclude with colonoscopy after an episode)
Irritable bowel syndrome (SCAD can mimic it)
Crohn's disease (diverticulitis can be confused with CD clinically and radiographically)
nonInfectiousMimics: Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis)
Giant sigmoid diverticulum (air-fluid level in LLQ on plain film)
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced abdominal/pelvic CT (diagnostic modality of choice for diverticulitis)
Multiplanar CT angiography for active diverticular bleeding localization
Nuclear medicine tagged red-cell scan for bleeding localization
Mesenteric angiography (allows superselective coil embolization if active bleeding is localized)
Colonoscopy ~6 weeks after resolution to exclude malignancy (avoid during the acute attack)
CRP and WBC count to gauge inflammation/disease progression risk
redFlags: Signs of peritonitis indicating diverticular perforation
Abscess formation (~16% of complicated disease) with abdominal distention and localized peritonitis
Free perforation with fecal peritonitis (Hinchey IV)
Air-fluid level in LLQ on plain film suggesting giant sigmoid diverticulum (impending perforation)
Massive or refractory lower-GI hemorrhage, hemodynamic instability, or large-volume transfusion requirement
Immunocompromise, chronic renal failure, or collagen-vascular disease (fivefold greater perforation risk on recurrent attacks)
harrison.prognosis: Most patients with diverticulosis stay asymptomatic; only ~5% develop acute diverticular disease, and 10-25% of those with diverticular disease have recurrent symptoms with up to 10% requiring surgery. Diverticular bleeds are largely self-limited (spontaneous cessation in >=90%), with lifetime rebleeding risk ~25%. After complicated diverticulitis the risk of underlying colon cancer rises to 6-8% (vs <2% overall). Elective surgical resection for recurrent SUDD improved quality of life and was more cost-effective at 5 years (DIRECT trial) (Harrison 22e p.2578-2581).
pitfalls: Do NOT perform colonoscopy during acute diverticulitis (risk of perforation); defer it ~6 weeks until the attack resolves.
Do not reflexively give antibiotics for uncomplicated diverticulitis in immunocompetent patients - trials show no benefit.
The historical advice to avoid nuts, corn, and popcorn rests on anecdotal data only and is not evidence-based; higher intake was actually associated with lower recurrence risk.
Mesalazine appears to help symptoms in SUDD but shows no benefit once objective inflammation (CRP, imaging) is considered.
A systematic review found no benefit to probiotics used alone.
Right-sided diverticula predominate in Asian populations, so a right-colon source should not be dismissed.
harrison.severityClassification: Hinchey classification of perforated diverticulitis: Stage I - perforation with confined paracolic abscess (modified stage Ia = phlegmon/early abscess); Stage II - perforation that closed spontaneously with distant (pelvic) abscess; Stage III - noncommunicating perforation with purulent peritonitis (diverticular neck closed off); Stage IV - free perforation communicating with the peritoneum producing fecal peritonitis. Clinically, disease is divided into uncomplicated (~75%) and complicated (~25%: abscess 16%, perforation 10%, stricture 5%, fistula 2%) (Harrison 22e p.2579-2580).
management: High-fibre diet and adequate hydration to lower intraluminal pressure and reduce the risk of symptomatic and recurrent disease

Acute uncomplicated diverticulitis managed with bowel rest and, where indicated, antibiotics covering Gram-negative and anaerobic organisms, though selected mild cases may be treated without antibiotics
Percutaneous drainage of a diverticular abscess and surgical resection (sigmoid colectomy) for complicated disease with perforation, obstruction, fistula or recurrent attacks

Acute diverticular bleeding managed with resuscitation and transfusion; most stop spontaneously, with colonoscopic haemostasis, superselective mesenteric embolisation or surgery for refractory bleeding
Analgesia while avoiding agents that impair colonic motility where feasible, with reintroduction of oral intake as symptoms settle
Colonoscopy after an acute attack has resolved to exclude malignancy, avoiding endoscopy during the acute phase
Monitor inflammatory markers and clinical response, escalating for surgical review if peritonism or deterioration develops
